n: Turned away by the Gergesenes, Jesus sails back across the Sea of Galilee to Capernaum, which Matthew calls “his own city” because Jesus made his home there.
Friends carry a paralyzed man to Jesus. Seeing their faith, Jesus speaks first to the man’s deepest need: forgiveness of sins.
Some scribes silently accuse Jesus of blasphemy, reasoning that only God can forgive sins. They are right about God — and wrong about Jesus.

f.g: blaspheme = speak irreverently of God or claim what belongs only to God.

n: Jesus reads their thoughts — itself a sign of who he is — and challenges their hidden accusation.

f.g: wherefore = why.

n: Anyone can claim to forgive sins, since no one can see it happen. Telling a paralyzed man to walk is easily tested.

f.g: whether = which of the two.

n: So Jesus does the visible miracle to prove the invisible one: the healing shows he truly has power to forgive sins.

f.w: power on earth to forgive sins

n: The man stands, picks up his mat, and walks home — living proof of Jesus’s authority.
The crowds respond with awe and praise God for giving such power to a man.
Jesus calls Matthew, a tax collector, from his tax booth. Matthew, the traditional author of this Gospel, leaves everything immediately.

f.g: The tax office or toll booth where duties were collected.
Also called Levi in Mark and Luke.

n: At a meal in Matthew’s house, many tax collectors and “sinners” eat with Jesus. Sharing a meal signaled acceptance and friendship.

f.g: Tax collectors who worked for Rome; Jews often viewed them as traitors and cheats.
sat at meat = reclined at a meal.

n: The Pharisees, who carefully avoided contact with sinners to stay ritually pure, are scandalized that Jesus would eat with such people.

f.g: A strict, influential Jewish group devoted to exact observance of the law and oral traditions.

n: Jesus answers with a proverb: doctors go where the sick are. He came for those who know they need healing.
Quoting Hosea, Jesus says God values mercy more than ritual. Ironically, those who think themselves righteous may not hear his call.

f.w: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice
not come to call the righteous

n: Disciples of John the Baptist ask why Jesus’s disciples don’t fast as they and the Pharisees regularly do.

f.g: Many Pharisees fasted twice a week.

n: Wedding guests don’t mourn while the groom is with them. Jesus is the Bridegroom; fasting will fit after he is taken away — a hint of his death.

f.g: The groom’s friends and wedding guests.

n: You don’t patch old cloth with unshrunk new fabric — it will pull away and tear worse. Jesus’s gospel isn’t just a patch on old traditions.

f.g: rent = tear.
Unshrunk cloth that would shrink when washed.

n: New wine expands as it ferments and would burst old, stiff leather wineskins. The new covenant needs new “containers” — renewed hearts and forms.

f.g: bottles = wineskins made of animal hide.

n: A synagogue ruler named Jairus (named in Mark and Luke) comes to Jesus. His daughter has just died, yet he believes Jesus can restore her.

f.g: A leader who oversaw synagogue services.

n: Jesus rises at once and goes with the grieving father, his disciples following.
On the way, a woman who has bled for twelve years — making her ritually unclean and isolated — reaches out and touches the edge of his clothing.

f.g: Continual bleeding, probably a menstrual disorder.
Likely the tassel (tzitzit) that observant Jewish men wore on their cloak corners.

n: She believes even a touch will heal her. Her faith is quiet and private, but very real.

f.g: whole = healed; the Greek word also means saved.

n: Jesus turns, calls her “Daughter,” and credits her faith. She is healed physically and publicly welcomed back.

f.w: thy faith hath made thee whole

n: At the ruler’s house, funeral mourners are already wailing and playing flutes, as was customary even for poor families.

f.g: Flute players hired for funeral mourning.

n: Jesus says the girl is only sleeping — death is not final in his presence. The mourners mock him, knowing she is dead.

f.g: Mocked him with ridicule.

n: Sending out the scoffers, Jesus takes her by the hand and she rises. It foreshadows his power over death itself.
News of the miracle spreads throughout the region.

f.g: The report of this event.

n: Two blind men follow Jesus, calling him “Son of David” — a messianic title. They recognize who he is even though they can’t see him.
Indoors, Jesus asks whether they believe he can heal them. Their simple answer: “Yea, Lord.”

f.w: Believe ye that I am able to do this?

n: Jesus touches their eyes and heals them according to their faith — a pattern repeated throughout these chapters.
Their sight returns. Jesus sternly tells them to keep quiet about it.

f.g: straitly = strictly, sternly.

n: Overjoyed, they tell everyone anyway, spreading his fame further.
As the healed men leave, people bring a man who cannot speak because of an evil spirit.

f.g: dumb = unable to speak.

n: When the spirit is cast out, the man speaks. The amazed crowds say nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel.

f.w: It was never so seen in Israel

n: The Pharisees can’t deny the miracle, so they attribute it to Satan. This accusation will return and be answered in chapter 12.
A summary of Jesus’s ministry: teaching, preaching, and healing in every town — almost word for word the same summary as 4:23, framing the section.
Jesus feels deep compassion for the crowds. They are exhausted and lost, like sheep with no shepherd to guide or protect them.

f.g: Greek splanchnizomai — a deep, gut-level feeling of pity.

n: He changes the image to a harvest: many people are ready to receive the gospel, but there are too few workers to gather them.
His answer is to pray for more laborers — and in the next chapter he sends out his own Twelve as answers to that prayer.
